questions.q: What is a debit memo primarily used for?
options: Billing a customer for something new that wasn't on the original invoice
Closing an underpaid invoice
Reducing a customer's balance
Merging two customer accounts
questions.explain: A debit memo stands on its own, billing for a new charge like a fee or correction, independent of any specific prior invoice.

questions.q: What two things happen when a chargeback is created in response to an underpayment?
options: Nothing happens until the customer pays the rest
The original invoice closes as fully applied, and a new debit item is created for the shortfall
The original invoice is deleted and a credit memo is issued
The customer's credit limit is automatically reduced
questions.explain: A chargeback closes the original invoice using the payment received plus the chargeback, and simultaneously creates a new, separately due debit item.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a chargeback and an adjustment, in the context of an $800 disputed deduction?
options: There is no difference; they produce identical accounting
A chargeback always writes off more than an adjustment would
A chargeback recreates the $800 as a new, collectible balance; an adjustment would write the $800 off entirely
An adjustment can only be used on credit memos
questions.explain: A chargeback keeps pursuing the disputed amount as still owed, while an adjustment removes it from the books as an accepted loss.

questions.q: A customer takes an unauthorized $300 deduction on an invoice, and the business disagrees with the deduction and still expects to collect it. Which transaction fits this situation?
options: A debit memo
An adjustment
A merge
A chargeback
questions.explain: Disputing a deduction and still expecting to collect it is exactly the chargeback scenario — closing the original invoice and recreating the amount as a new item.

questions.q: Is a debit memo typically linked to a specific original invoice the way a chargeback is?
options: No — a debit memo usually stands on its own as a new amount owed
Yes, always — a debit memo cannot exist without an original invoice
Only if AutoInvoice created it
Only for credit card transactions
questions.explain: Unlike a chargeback, which is explicitly tied to closing an existing invoice, a debit memo is generally a standalone new charge.
